source.subject: Biology
source.unit: Unit 1 — Diversity in the Living World
source.source_scope: Only the content printed on PDF page 3: Chapter 1 opening passage and the beginning of section 1.1, Diversity in the Living World.

questions.question: What is the title of Chapter 1?
questions.explanation: The page heading identifies Chapter 1 as The Living World.

questions.question: Which two sections are listed in the chapter contents on this page?
options: Diversity in the Living World and Taxonomic Categories
questions.explanation: The page lists sections 1.1 Diversity in the Living World and 1.2 Taxonomic Categories.
questions.source_text: 1.1 Diversity in the Living World; 1.2 Taxonomic Categories

questions.question: Which of the following habitats is explicitly mentioned in the opening passage?
questions.explanation: Cold mountains are one of the habitats listed in the passage.
questions.source_text: cold mountains, deciduous forests, oceans, fresh water lakes, deserts or hot springs

questions.question: Which habitats are mentioned as places where living organisms are found?
questions.explanation: The passage lists deciduous forests, fresh water lakes, deserts and hot springs, among other habitats.
questions.source_text: deciduous forests, oceans, fresh water lakes, deserts or hot springs

questions.question: Which examples are used in the passage to evoke awe and a deep sense of wonder?
questions.explanation: The passage names a galloping horse, migrating birds, the valley of flowers and an attacking shark.
questions.source_text: The beauty of a galloping horse, of the migrating birds, the valley of flowers or the attacking shark evokes awe and a deep sense of wonder.

questions.question: The passage refers to ecological conflict and cooperation among members of a population and among:
questions.explanation: The text mentions ecological conflict and cooperation among populations of a community.
questions.source_text: among members of a population and among populations of a community

questions.question: Besides ecological interactions, what process inside a cell is mentioned in the opening passage?
questions.explanation: The passage refers to molecular traffic inside a cell.
questions.source_text: the molecular traffic inside a cell

questions.question: The first implicit question within the question ‘what is life?’ is described as:
options: A technical question about what is living as opposed to non-living
A philosophical question about the purpose of life
A question about the origin of the universe
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes the technical question of living versus non-living from the philosophical question about life's purpose.
questions.source_text: The first is a technical one and seeks answer to what living is as opposed to the non-living

questions.question: According to the passage, the second implicit question concerns:
questions.explanation: The second question is described as philosophical and concerned with the purpose of life.
questions.source_text: the second is a philosophical one, and seeks answer to what the purpose of life is

questions.question: Which question does the passage say scientists will try to reflect on?
options: What is the purpose of life?
questions.explanation: The passage says scientists will not attempt to answer the philosophical question about life's purpose, but will reflect on what is living.
questions.source_text: As scientists, we shall not attempt answering the second question. We will try to reflect on – what is living?

questions.question: Which examples of living organisms are mentioned in section 1.1?
options: Only organisms visible to the naked eye
questions.explanation: The passage names potted plants, insects, birds, pets and other animals and plants; it also notes that some organisms cannot be seen with the naked eye.
questions.source_text: potted plants, insects, birds, your pets or other animals and plants

questions.question: According to section 1.1, what happens to the range and variety of organisms observed when the area of observation increases?
options: All organisms become visible to the naked eye
questions.explanation: The passage states that increasing the area of observation increases the range and variety of organisms seen.
questions.source_text: If you were to increase the area that you make observations in, the range and variety of organisms that you see would increase.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest one would probably observe on visiting a dense forest?
options: A greater number and kinds of living organisms
No organisms that cannot be seen with the naked eye
Fewer kinds of organisms than in a smaller area
questions.explanation: The text says a dense forest would probably show a much greater number and kinds of living organisms.
questions.source_text: if you were to visit a dense forest, you would probably see a much greater number and kinds of living organisms in it

questions.question: According to section 1.1, each different kind of plant, animal or organism that one sees represents a:
questions.explanation: The passage states that each different kind of plant, animal or organism represents a species.
questions.source_text: Each different kind of plant, animal or organism that you see, represents a species.

questions.question: The number of species known and described is stated on this page to range between:
questions.explanation: The page gives the range as 1.7–1.8 million and relates it to biodiversity.
questions.source_text: The number of species that are known and described range between 1.7-1.8 million.
